properties.name: A deliberate startup refusal reaches the MCP client as CONNECT_TIMEOUT, because reflow2's readiness deadline and the client's connect timeout are both 30 seconds
properties.statement:
THE SYMPTOM AS OBSERVED (dev_storyflow, 2026-09-08): `CONNECT_TIMEOUT after 30000ms`, no reflow2 tools for a whole session, while `.reflow2/graph.server.log` held the precise reason — a graph written by reflow2 0.50.0 refused by 0.55.1. The reporter's own words: 'It is not a connection problem at all... Every diagnostic instinct that timeout provokes is wrong, and the correct message was sitting in a log nobody had reason to open.'

CANDIDATES CONSIDERED, five: (1) the --serve-shared daemon exits on every open failure, so no rendezvous ever appears; (2) reflow2's READY_TIMEOUT equals the client's connect timeout, so nothing said after it can be heard; (3) the daemon's stderr goes to a log file and never reaches the session, so even a correct message has no path; (4) not-in-the-suspected-component — the peer's launch wrapper swallowed the output; (5) the observation is wrong and CONNECT_TIMEOUT came from something else.

THE DISCRIMINATING MEASUREMENT, taken 2026-09-09 against a real permanently-unopenable store: drive `--shared` as an MCP client and time the handshake reply. Candidate 3 predicts NO reply; candidates 1 and 2 predict a correct degraded reply, late.

RESULT: the handshake arrived at **t+30.0 s**, carrying the correct, complete degraded surface with the reason in its instructions. So candidate 3 is REFUTED — the machinery was right all along — and 1 and 2 are both true. They are not separable by timing (both predict 30 s), and they are separable by consequence: 1 explains why no rendezvous appears, 2 explains why the correct answer is unreachable anyway. READY_TIMEOUT is 30 s and the client gives up at 30 s. It is a dead heat the client always wins.

THE CLASS, not the instance: the version guard was the trigger. The cause is that the `--serve-shared` daemon handles EVERY open failure with the path written for ONE of them. Losing the store-lock race means somebody else won and will publish; a version-guard refusal, a corrupt store or an unreadable path mean there is no winner and never will be. The waiting loop's own comment justifies the wait by assuming a winner exists, and never notices that assumption.

⭐ AND SHORTENING THE DEADLINE IS NOT THE FIX — this is the measurement that killed the obvious answer. `fact:the-first-store-read-of-a-session-costs-26-to-48-seconds` measured a LEGITIMATE cold daemon start at ~26 s, so 30 s already carries four seconds of headroom. Cutting it would trade a bricked graph's bad message for a healthy graph's false one. The reason has to travel instead of the clock being moved.

WHAT WAS BUILT: the daemon records a refusal beside the store (`<graph>.server.refused.json`, the same sidecar convention as the rendezvous) when its failure is one no peer can resolve; the spawning session stops waiting the instant it reads one written by a pid it spawned. Measured after: **t+30.0 s becomes t+0.3 s**, and the handshake instructions name the actual refusal.

PINNED, AND OBSERVED TO FAIL FIRST: `tools/test_degraded_server.py::SharedRefusalIsNotATimeoutTest`, 4 cases. Against the unfixed binary, 3 fail — the timing case at 30.024 s, the message case because the old text said 'within 30s' and blamed the write lock, and the record case because nothing was written. The fourth, `a_lost_lock_race_still_waits_for_the_winner`, passes in BOTH states: it is the counterweight, and it fails if the fix is ever widened into a blanket 'any open failure means stop waiting'.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH: the reproduction used a forged future stamp and a permanently-held lock, not the reporter's retired-type case, which cannot be constructed any more — a retired type is by definition one this binary will not write. Both drive the identical guard branch and the identical refusal, so the path is the same; the exact 0.50.0 store was never re-run. The 30 s client timeout is taken from the reporter's message and from this session's own measurement of when the reply arrives; no client's configuration was inspected. And the ~26 s legitimate cold start is quoted from an August measurement of a 77 MB store, not re-measured here.
